title: Kernel handoff latency surge: root cause analysis, mitigations, and hardening plan
creator: Ava Chen
body:
Summary:
On 2026-03-09 18:20 UTC we observed a sustained p95 and p99 latency increase (2x-3x) across multiple hosted clusters serving short-sequence chat workloads. The incident correlated with a scheduler rollout (canary -> region) that enabled aggressive kernel probing and an attention autotiling change introduced earlier that week. Root cause analysis shows an interaction between the scheduler's probe-driven handoff logic and the autotiler which produced frequent kernel handoffs for short sequences, causing KV-cache churn and transient CPU/GPU stalls during warmup.

Timeline (high level):
- 2026-03-08 02:00: attention-autotile enabled in canary (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1156)
- 2026-03-09 12:00: scheduler probe heuristics rolled to region (feature flag rollout)
- 2026-03-09 18:20: first customer complaints of elevated tail latency; internal alerts fired (p95 > 2x baseline)
- 2026-03-09 18:35: Ops throttled new routing to fallback path; partial rollback of scheduler flag started
- 2026-03-10 04:00: temporary mitigations in place; incident declared resolved for immediate customer impact but follow-up required

Root cause (detailed):
- The scheduler's probe window mechanism intermittently prefers kernel variants based on recent samples; this probing was tuned to be aggressive to surface lower-cost kernels quickly.
- Attention autotiling changes introduced a new execution path that is optimal for medium sequence lengths but for short sequences triggers extra kernel module boundaries. Short queries caused frequent kernel handoffs.
- Kernel handoffs reset or partially invalidate the runtime's KV cache state in some code paths (edge case in cache sync logic). The combined effect: increased micro-warmups, more kernel context switches, higher host-side copying, and spikes in GPU kernel launch latency for p95/p99.
- The fault surface was amplified during capacity surge because probing frequency increased and probe failures caused back-off that misaligned with autoscaling, producing transient queueing and further tail amplification.

Immediate mitigations applied (completed):
- Rolled back scheduler probe rollout to conservative configuration in the affected region (feature flag reverted) — mitigated majority of tail spikes.
- Rolled back attention-autotile toggle to previous safe path in canary until a hardened autotile is available.
- Applied a short-term patch to KV-cache sync code to reduce invalidations on kernel handoff (hotfix PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1234).
- Added emergency dashboard alert that correlates kernel handoff rate with KV-cache invalidations and queue lengths (Dashboard: https://monitoring.redwood.ai/d/hand-off).

Decisions made and trade-offs:
- Revert autotile rather than attempt a quick in-production patch: safe but sacrifices potential cost/throughput wins from autotile in the short term.
- Prefer deterministic mapping with slower probe cadence for p99 stability; this costs some exploration for lower-cost kernels but preserves SLOs.
- Short-term KV-cache patch reduces invalidations at the cost of slightly more memory retention which is acceptable for high-tail stability.

Action plan (owners, estimates, due dates):
- A. Scheduler probe hardening (owner: Marcus Rivera, estimate: 5):
  - Implement probe feathering: reduce probe frequency for short sequences, add probe budget per runtime instance.
  - Add probe hysteresis and versioned kernel-mapping cache to avoid oscillation during capacity changes.
  - Due: 2026-03-24

- B. Kernel handoff prewarm and KV-cache contract (owner: Priya Singh, estimate: 8):
  - Define and implement a handoff prewarm handshake (preload small amount of KV state) and explicit cache-contracts between kernel variants to avoid full invalidation on handoff.
  - Add unit tests and microbenchmarks validating cache semantics across kernel variants.
  - Due: 2026-04-07

- C. Autotile redesign for short-sequence workloads (owner: Daniel Kim, estimate: 13):
  - Rework autotile decision graph to avoid creating additional kernel boundaries for sequences < 64 tokens.
  - Introduce telemetry flags to measure kernel boundary counts and attach to cost/latency dashboards.
  - Due: 2026-04-21

- D. Observability and runbook updates (owner: Ava Chen, estimate: 3):
  - Add spans for kernel handoff events, explicit KV-cache invalidation traces, and attach token-count metadata.
  - Update incident runbook with steps to identify kernel handoff storms and recommended temporary flag toggles.
  - Due: 2026-03-20

- E. Canary/Load testing: continuous mixed-quant benchmark (owner: Soren Patel, estimate: 8):
  - Add a nightly mixed-quant, short-sequence benchmark suite to catch regressions where kernel-per-request overhead dominates.
  - Integrate with PR gating for scheduler/autotile changes.
  - Due: 2026-04-15

Review feedback and approvals:
- PM review (Priya): Approved prioritization for scheduler hardening over autotile optimizations until stability is verifiably restored.
- Design/Perf review (Daniel): Suggested additional microbenchmarks focusing on kernel boundary count distribution rather than only p95 latency.
- Security: No secrets or auth changes; security review not required.

Follow-ups and monitoring criteria (done when):
- p95 and p99 for short-sequence chat across affected clusters return to within 10% of baseline for two rolling weeks.
- Kernel handoff rate decreases > 80% compared to peak incident rate for short-sequence traffic under similar load.
- KV-cache invalidation events decrease > 95% in correlation during handoffs.

Artifacts and references:
- Hotfix PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1234
- Autotile original PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1156
- Incident dashboard: https://monitoring.redwood.ai/d/hand-off
- Postmortem doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/ENG-559001+kernel-handoff-retro

Notes and lessons learned:
- Aggressive probing is a plausible source of tail amplification when combined with short-sequence micro-optimizations. Feature flags and phased canaries should include a short-sequence workload bucket and mixed-quant stress tests.
- Kernel boundary counts are a useful metric for predicting KV-cache churn; adding lightweight telemetry here will improve MTTR for similar regressions.
- Capacity events and probe-driven decisions interact non-linearly; autoscaling signals should be part of probe budget calculations.
